author: haiku
reason: A opens with a one-paragraph summary, then gives numbered steps, each with what triggers it and what happens on failure, plus a failure table showing whether budget is used; B spreads the same flow across a long glossary and a list of design decisions, cites "requirement N" items the reader never sees, and contradicts itself on the Enterprise path, so A is quicker and more reliable to understand despite its escaped-newline formatting.

author: haiku
reason: B is clearer: it opens with a short summary, then gives numbered steps and a failure table that shows the client response and whether budget is used in each case. author: haiku
reason: B is quicker to understand: it uses plain terms (source, mirror, replica, idempotent), explains its key design choices before the steps, and defines one switch procedure that it reuses for cutover, rollback and finish, while A asks a newcomer to hold dense jargon and separate procedures (fence, owner/mode, write_owner fallback, distinct rollback steps) to follow the same flow.

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term in plain language, describes one reusable switch procedure with explicit pause, commit point and abort/roll-forward rules, and gives every step the same Starts/Does/State/If-it-fails layout, while B makes a newcomer juggle denser terms (owner/mode/paused, a fallback write_owner flag), name inconsistencies like "Phase 0 build" against Phases A/B/C, and separate hand-written switch and rollback sequences.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer the mental model first (a source of truth and a follower that swap roles, and every write as commit, then a quick copy, then repair), groups the steps into phases, and lists Starts/Changes/State/If it fails the same way for every step, while A puts a dense block of SQL-level rules ahead of the steps, so the engineer has to absorb that detail before seeing the flow.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A opens with the core write mechanism (commit with an outbox row, then a quick copy, then drainer repair) and runs the same mechanism in reverse at the switch, and every step uses the same Starts/Changes/State/If it fails layout, so a newcomer gets the model quickly; Document B's single write-mode flag and state table are neat, but its long, mode-by-mode rules section is harder to absorb.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a newcomer more of what they need to follow the system end to end: it defines the basic terms (ledger, payment provider, charge key), labels each mode inside the diagram, explains how to read the diagram, and lists the rollback steps separately for each starting mode with a clear place for the fence and step state. A is tighter, but it leaves core mechanics open, such as how the freeze is seen and whether idempotency exists, so the reader understands the flow less fully, even allowing for B's repetition and its slip that a rollback "returns to shadow".

author: haiku
reason: Document A makes the mechanism concrete: a fence flag in a durable rollout record, a charge key checked against the ledger before every charge, and separate rollback sequences for each starting mode. Document B has a crisp summary and a clean failure table, but it leaves central mechanics as open questions, such as how workers see the freeze while the flag still names the new engine and whether the idempotency key exists at all, and it contradicts itself on whether workers cache the flag.

author: sonnet
reason: B is quicker for a newcomer to follow because it defines the basic terms (ledger, provider, billing period), labels every diagram state in plain words, gives a separate rollback path for each starting mode, lists the four possible reconcile outcomes and names the concrete double-charge guards (idempotency key and ledger uniqueness), while A packs similar content into dense table cells and a more involved blocked-and-restart-from-Reconcile flow, even though A is more complete about who runs the rollback.

author: sonnet
